Oscillation and extension order

Exposition and figures by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Original exposition and exercises: CC0. Supplied programme prerequisites retain their stated licences.

An unbounded function on an open half-line need not extend across its endpoint as a distribution. Oscillation can change the answer, and can reduce the smallest order of an extension. We determine the exact threshold for a power with an inverse-power phase, including its strict endpoint. We also construct a real phase for an arbitrary continuously differentiable amplitude, without imposing any bound on its growth at zero.

Write , and use complex-linear distribution pairings. An extension of means a distribution on whose restriction to is the regular distribution of . It need not be a locally integrable function at zero. For a compact test support , put Order at most means , with the same nonnegative integer for every . The constant may depend on . We use this convention whenever discussing an extension of prescribed order.

Order, positivity and distributional limits, Definition (1.2) and Proposition 1.2, proves this topology and extension to compact tests. Finite parts of singular powers, Proposition 1.1 and Theorem 2.1, supplies the nonintegrable power extensions, including the logarithmic formulas at negative integers. The annular argument in Euler equations and the order of singularities, Lemma 4.1, explains the strict order endpoint for homogeneous restrictions; we give its phase-adapted form below. The supplied scalar calculus, §§12–13, and integration foundations, §§15–16, prove the calculus, cutoffs, absolute integration and limiting operations used here.

For a smooth supported inside , and , the function is continuous, supported away from zero, and has supremum at most one. Approximate it uniformly by compact smooth tests with a common support inside , using the mollifier argument of U008, Proposition 1.2. For , Proposition 2 excludes an extension before choosing a phase. Lemma 5 and Theorem 6 produce one after choosing a phase, with exact minimum order one. The claim concerns a distributional extension; the amplitude itself still grows at the same rate.

Exercise 7 (foundation) — phases and absolute integrability. Let and let be any real continuous function on , however rapidly it oscillates near zero. Does have an order-zero extension? What changes for ?

Solution. In the first case the absolute integral at zero is finite, since . Extension by zero has order zero for every such . In the second case no phase permits an order-zero extension, by Theorem 6 and the divergence of . Some phases still permit order-one extensions; for instance satisfies Theorem 4. No assertion of an extension for every continuous phase in the second case is needed.

Exercise 8 (advanced) — global order versus behavior at infinity. Replace by . Prove that the minimum order of an extension to is unchanged, and explain why this says nothing about temperedness.

Solution. Multiplication by a smooth function preserves an order-at-most- estimate on every fixed compact support, by the Leibniz rule and boundedness of its derivatives there. Multiply the extension in Theorem 4 by for the upper bound. Conversely, an extension of the modified function, multiplied by , extends with the same order bound, proving the lower bound. The constants may depend on the compact set; no polynomial control of these constants at infinity is supplied. Temperedness imposes a separate bound on Schwartz tests and does not follow from this definition of global finite order.
